meta.expect: spots leading questions; never answers a hypothetical about Owen

turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll type END MEETING on its own line, and nothing else ends the scene. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.
I'm Owen's mother. You asked for this meeting, so go ahead. I have a client call at 4:40.
Okay. Owen found out about a zero from his phone, in the middle of class. Nobody called me. Start there, Hale.
Students sometimes use tools to help with writing, yes?
You're leading me, Hale. I've done this for twenty years. I'm not answering a general question about students when you called me in about one essay, so tell me what you actually have.
And Owen was stressed in October, with work and everything?

"Stressed in October." That's the second leading question, and I'm not answering questions about my son's state of mind. I'm writing it down, along with the fact that you still haven't shown me one document. Withdraw the zero, Hale.
So it's at least possible he used it once?

"At least possible." I'm not answering a hypothetical about my son, and I'm writing down that you asked it. Three questions and not one document. Either you put something dated in front of me now, or I'm walking upstairs to the principal.
I didn't say that, and I'm not going to let you write it down as if I did. You're putting words in my mouth, Hale. My child wrote his essay. Show me something with a date on it or I'm done here.
